title: Classifying Action Items for Semantic Email
research_question: Can action items in email be automatically classified into useful semantic categories using a computationally tractable speech-act model and linguistic rules?
methodology: The authors define email action items using three dimensions: action, object, and subject, producing a taxonomy that distinguishes requests, assignments, suggestions, and deliveries over tasks, events, information, and resources. They implement a rule-based classifier in GATE using tokenization, sentence splitting, POS tagging, gazetteers, named-entity processing, semantic and grammatical features, and JAPE speech-act grammars. The system is evaluated by 12 people on 116 emails, with evaluators judging automatically identified items and adding missed items.

key_findings.finding: The proposed model represents action items through action, object, and subject dimensions and yields 22 basic action-item combinations.
The implemented classifier uses modality, verb category, tense, negation, and semantic-role information, with additional rules for phenomena such as conditional constructions.
An earlier human annotation exercise over the 22-category scheme achieved inter-annotator agreement of 0.811, indicating substantial but imperfect agreement on the task.
In the reported evaluation, the rule-based classifier achieved precision 0.56, recall 0.60, and F1 0.58.
The authors conclude that the classifier is not reliable enough for unattended automatic annotation and is better used to suggest candidate annotations for user review and correction.

limitations: The linguistic model and implementation are designed for English-language email.
The evaluation contains only 116 emails and 194 automatically classified action items, so it is not a large standardized benchmark.
The reported F1 score of 0.58 leaves substantial false-positive and false-negative error.
The approach depends on manually engineered linguistic and JAPE rules and is therefore potentially brittle under new wording or domains.
The model represents actor participation and broad action semantics but does not provide a dedicated deadline field comparable to structured action-item extraction schemas.
The paper does not report release of the task-specific evaluation corpus or the complete rule set as a reusable research artifact.
raw_claims: The action-item representation separates the type of action from its semantic object and participating subject.
The four principal action types are request, assign, suggest, and deliver.
Tasks and events are treated as activity objects, while information and resources are treated as data objects.
The classifier incorporates grammatical modality, verb semantics, tense, negation, and semantic roles.
The JAPE speech-act component alone contains 58 rules arranged in 14 phases.
The evaluation involved 12 people reviewing at least eight emails each.
Evaluators assessed 194 automatically classified action items and manually added 74 missed items.
The reported precision, recall, and F1 are 0.56, 0.60, and 0.58 respectively.
The authors propose using corrected rule-based output later as training material for machine-learning approaches.
